claims.text: The target material is a homogeneous, single-phase, quaternary equiatomic FCC alloy with moderate stacking-fault energy.
Sufficiently high stacking-fault energy suppresses deformation twinning in the target alloy.
Sufficiently high stacking-fault energy suppresses stress-induced phase transformation in the target alloy.
When twinning and phase transformation are suppressed, dislocation glide is the sole rate-controlling deformation mechanism.
Dislocation forest density dominates plastic flow under the proposed high-SFE conditions.
Lattice-friction stress dominates plastic flow under the proposed high-SFE conditions.
At 300–500 K, dislocation glide is controlled by lattice diffusion and forest hardening.
Thermally activated mechanisms such as cross-slip saturate at intermediate temperatures.
Saturation of cross-slip produces a plateau in strain-rate sensitivity.
Low-temperature deformation may be dominated by twinning or an FCC-to-HCP phase transformation.
At high temperature, diffusion-controlled creep takes over from the intermediate-temperature mechanism.
The strain-rate sensitivity exponent has a distinct plateau between 300 and 500 K.
Yield strength remains constant as strain rate increases from approximately 10^-4 to 10^-1 s^-1 in the plateau regime.
Below the plateau regime, strain-rate sensitivity increases because of twinning or phase transformation.
Above the plateau regime, strain-rate sensitivity decreases because of creep.
Conventional FCC alloys typically exhibit a monotonic increase in yield strength with strain rate because dislocation motion is thermally activated.
Low-SFE alloys are dominated by twinning at all strain rates.
The hypothesis requires applied stress to remain below a critical threshold for pressure-induced HCP transformation.
The temperature range of the proposed plateau depends on the alloy's stacking-fault energy.
The hypothesis is falsified if no plateau occurs over 300–600 K or if HCP transformation or twinning occurs in the predicted plateau regime.
